claim: Ctp was significantly enriched in immunoprecipitations of GFP-tagged Panx and Nxf2 from ovary lysates.
source: As well as known components of the PICTS complex, the protein Cut-up (Ctp) was significantly enriched in both experiments (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1A, which displays enrichment of Ctp in both GFP-Panx and GFP-Nxf2 IPs.

claim: Ctp is a member of the LC8 family of dynein light chains and a component of the dynein motor complex.
source: This was an unexpected result, since Ctp is a member of the LC8 family of dynein light chains and a component of the dynein motor complex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Ctp's identity and function.

claim: Ctp is ubiquitously expressed, in contrast to Piwi, Panx, and Nxf2 which display ovary-enriched expression.
source: Moreover, in contrast to Piwi, Panx, and Nxf2, which display ovary-enriched expression, Ctp is ubiquitously expressed (Figure 1B) and essential for viability, with loss-of-function mutations in Drosophila causing embryonic lethality (Dick et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1B and cited literature (Dick et al., 1996) regarding lethality.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in ctp cause embryonic lethality in Drosophila.
source: Moreover, in contrast to Piwi, Panx, and Nxf2, which display ovary-enriched expression, Ctp is ubiquitously expressed (Figure 1B) and essential for viability, with loss-of-function mutations in Drosophila causing embryonic lethality (Dick et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dick et al., 1996.

claim: Drosophila Ctp differs by only four amino acids from its mammalian ortholog.
source: The LC8 family of dynein light chains was first identified as a component of cytoplasmic dynein (King and Patel-King, 1995) and this family is extremely well conserved, with Drosophila Ctp differing by only four amino acids from its mammalian ortholog (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and cited literature (King and Patel-King, 1995).

claim: Germline-specific shRNA-mediated knockdown of ctp resulted in significant de-repression of the germline-specific transposons HeTA and burdock.
source: Similarly to Panx, germ cell-specific shRNA-mediated knockdown of ctp resulted in significant de-repression of the germline-specific transposons HeTA and burdock, assayed by qPCR (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 71.0% of transposon families were significantly upregulated upon depletion of Ctp in the germline.
source: We found that 49 out of 69 (71.0%) transposon families were significantly upregulated upon depletion of Ctp (Figure 1D) indicating that loss of Ctp impairs transposon repression in the germline.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Germline knockdown of Panx resulted in de-repression of 19.4% of transposon families.
source: This effect was stronger than germline knockdown of Panx, which resulted in de-repression of 19.4% of transposon families (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Ctp loss had a strong effect on gene expression, with 2578 (or 16.2%) genes changing more than fourfold compared to the control.
source: Unlike Panx (63 or 0.5% genes), Ctp loss also had a strong effect on gene expression, with 2578 (or 16.2%) genes changing more than fourfold compared to the control.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis comparing ctp knockdown to control.

claim: Piwi nuclear localisation was unaffected upon ctp germline knockdown.
source: Piwi nuclear localisation was unaffected upon ctp germline knockdown (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and piRNA levels were only moderately changed in ovarian somatic cells depleted of Ctp (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), both consistent with the knockdown of a protein involved in TGS.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: piRNA levels were only moderately changed in ovarian somatic cells depleted of Ctp.
source: Piwi nuclear localisation was unaffected upon ctp germline knockdown (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and piRNA levels were only moderately changed in ovarian somatic cells depleted of Ctp (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), both consistent with the knockdown of a protein involved in TGS.
evidence: This is supported by small RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Germline depletion of Ctp resulted in a severe disruption of the ovary morphology with most ovarioles lacking late-stage egg chambers.
source: However, germline depletion of Ctp resulted in a severe disruption of the ovary morphology with most ovarioles lacking late-stage egg chambers (Figure 1G), likely reflecting the requirement of this protein for a number of cellular processes (Barbar, 2008; Rapali et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI staining images shown in Figure 1G and cited literature (Barbar, 2008; Rapali et al., 2011b).

claim: Females with Ctp depleted in germ cells failed to lay eggs.
source: Indeed, females with Ctp depleted in germ cells failed to lay eggs, while germline knockdown of panx resulted in sterility with only a minimal effect on egg laying (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by fertility assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 37 transposon families were strongly upregulated upon ctp knockdown in OSCs.
source: Overall, 37 transposon families were strongly upregulated (log2 fold-change >2, RPKM >1, adjusted p value < 0.05) upon ctp knockdown, including both soma-specific transposons such as gypsy and 297, and transposons active in both the germline and soma, such as 412 and blood (Figure 2A,C,F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A, C, and F.

claim: Knockdown of ctp had a greater impact on non-transposon gene expression compared to knockdown of panx, nxf2, or piwi in OSCs.
source: In line with this and consistent with the germline phenotype, knockdown of ctp had a greater impact on non-transposon gene expression, with 354 out of 15,644 (2.7%) genes changing significantly, compared to 0.7%, 0.6%, and 1.0% for siPanx, siNxf2, and siPiwi, respectively (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Up to half of the upregulated genes in ctp, panx, nxf2, and piwi knockdowns reside in genomic locations with their promoters within close proximity of a gypsy, mdg1, blood, 297 or 412 insertion.
source: Remarkably, in all four knockdowns up to half of the upregulated genes reside in genomic locations with their promoters within close proximity of a gypsy, mdg1, blood, 297 or 412 insertion (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that some of the observed gene expression changes are a pleiotropic effect caused by a failure in transposon silencing.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The most highly upregulated genes are more likely to be in genomic proximity to a transposon than those that are changing weakly.
source: Moreover, analysis of these genes in terms of fold-change revealed that the most highly upregulated genes are more likely to be in genomic proximity to a transposon than those that are changing weakly (Figure 2E), further indicating that piRNA pathway disruption is driving the strongest gene expression changes observed in these knockdowns.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Loss of Ctp resulted in a severe reduction of the H3K9me3 mark across de-repressed transposon sequences including gypsy and 297.
source: Loss of Ctp resulted in a severe reduction of the H3K9me3 mark across de-repressed transposon sequences including gyspy and 297, in a similar manner to that observed upon siPanx, siNxf2, or siPiwi, which correlated with increased read coverage from RNA-seq (Figure 2F,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2F, G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Ctp depletion resulted in an almost complete loss of the H3K9me3 coverage from the genomic region surrounding gypsy and 297 insertions.
source: Analysis of the H3K9me3 signal surrounding gypsy and 297 insertions in the OSC genome revealed that Ctp depletion resulted in an almost complete loss of the H3K9me3 coverage from the genomic region surrounding each insertion (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Loss of H3K9me3 correlated with an increase in the coverage of H3K4me2 across gypsy and 297 insertions.
source: Moreover, this correlated with an increase in the coverage of H3K4me2, a mark indicative of active transcription, across the same insertions (Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Knockdown of PICTS complex components resulted in significant enrichment for H3K4me2 and depletion of H3K9me3 around gypsy, mdg1, blood, 297, or 412 insertions.
source: When considering ChIP-seq signal around all gypsy, mdg1, blood, 297, or 412 insertions in the OSC genome, we detected a significant enrichment for H3K4me2 and depletion of H3K9me3 upon knockdown of PICTS complex components, while control regions (those surrounding unaffected transposons and heterochromatic regions on chromosome 4) were only marginally affected (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: 3xFLAG-Ctp displayed both cytoplasmic and nuclear localisation in OSCs.
source: Consistent with a function in chromatin silencing, 3xFLAG-Ctp displayed both cytoplasmic and nuclear localisation in OSCs that was not perturbed upon knockdown of panx (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of panx did not affect the distribution or stability of endogenous Ctp.
source: Fractionation experiments from OSCs treated with siGFP confirmed the presence of Ctp in both nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments, with knockdown of panx not affecting the distribution or stability of endogenous Ctp (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Depletion of Ctp resulted in a reduction of Panx protein levels.
source: However, depletion of Ctp resulted in a reduction of Panx protein levels, albeit not as severe as observed following knockdown of nxf2 (Figure 3C), as reported previously (Batki et al., 2019; Fabry et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C and cited literature (Batki et al., 2019; Fabry et al., 2019).

claim: Tethering of λN-Panx to RNA induced strong silencing of the reporter at both the protein level and the RNA level.
source: Tethering of λN-Panx to RNA induced strong silencing of the reporter, both at the protein level (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C) and the RNA level (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) when compared to the λN-Renilla control, as reported (Batki et al., 2019; Fabry et al., 2019; Murano et al., 2019; Sienski et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C, D, and cited literature.

claim: Transfection of λN-Ctp resulted in reporter repression at comparable levels to λN-Panx, with 28% ZsGreen protein and 29% nascent transcript signal remaining relative to the λN-Renilla control.
source: Transfection of λN-Ctp also resulted in reporter repression at comparable levels to λN-Panx, with 28% ZsGreen protein and 29% nascent transcript signal remaining relative to the λN-Renilla control (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D), indicating that Ctp can also function as a co-transcriptional repressor in OSCs.
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: Tethering of Ctp to DNA resulted in potent reporter repression with 10% ZsGreen protein and 4% ZsGreen transcript signal remaining relative to the control.
source: Moreover, tethering of Ctp to DNA resulted in potent reporter repression to a similar extent as tethering of Panx (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F) with 10% ZsGreen protein and 4% ZsGreen transcript signal remaining relative to the control.
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: DNA recruitment of Ctp resulted in potent repression in the germ cell compartment of the fly ovary.
source: In addition, use of an in vivo DNA tethering reporter showed that, like Panx, DNA recruitment of Ctp resulted in potent repression, indicating that Ctp can also function as a transcriptional repressor in the germ cell compartment of the fly ovary (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo reporter assay data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of 3xFLAG-Ctp from OSCs confirmed the interaction between Ctp and Panx, Nxf2 and Nxt1.
source: In order to understand how Ctp contributes to Piwi-dependent transposon control, we performed immunoprecipitation of 3xFLAG-Ctp from OSCs and analysed recovered proteins by mass spectrometry. This confirmed the interaction between Ctp and Panx, Nxf2 and Nxt1 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by IP-MS data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Piwi was not found enriched in the Ctp immunoprecipitation.
source: Of note, we did not find Piwi enriched (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) consistent with results arising from immunoprecipitations of other members of PICTS (Batki et al., 2019; Fabry et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by IP-MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and cited literature (Batki et al., 2019; Fabry et al., 2019).

claim: The interaction between Ctp and Panx is mediated by the carboxy-terminal region of Panx.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments in OSCs showed that the interaction between Ctp and Panx is mediated by the carboxy-terminal region of Panx (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A Panx mutant lacking the second coiled coil region (PanxΔCC2+deg) was still able to bind Ctp.
source: A Panx mutant lacking the second coiled coil region (PanxΔCC2+deg), which fails to interact with Nxf2 (Fabry et al., 2019), was still able to bind Ctp (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the Panx-Ctp interaction is independent of Nxf2.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and cited literature (Fabry et al., 2019).

claim: Ctp and Nxf2 were only found to associate in the presence of Panx.
source: In contrast, Ctp and Nxf2 were only found to associate in the presence of Panx (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), pointing toward a direct interaction between Ctp and Panx, with Panx serving as an interaction platform for PICTS complex components.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 32 proteins enriched in the Ctp IP-MS contain one or more putative TQT motifs.
source: Among all 59 proteins enriched in the Ctp IP-MS, we identified 32 proteins with one or more putative TQT motifs (Figure 4C,D and Supplementary file 1) using the binding sequence prediction tool LC8Pred (Jespersen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by analysis using LC8Pred shown in Figure 4C, D and Supplementary file 1, and cited literature (Jespersen et al., 2019).

claim: Panx contains two highly scoring and conserved TQT recognition sequences in the C-terminus.
source: Strikingly, this included two highly scoring and conserved recognition sequences in the C-terminus of Panx (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by LC8Pred analysis and sequence conservation shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mutation of both TQT motifs in Panx entirely abolishes the interaction with Ctp.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation analysis in OSCs revealed that both PanxTQT#1 and PanxTQT#2 have a reduced ability to interact with Ctp, but only mutation of both sites entirely abolishes the interaction (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Panx2xTQT was still able to interact with Nxf2.
source: Panx2xTQT was still able to interact with Nxf2, supporting that the interactions of Panx with Nxf2 and with Ctp are independent (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The wild-type Panx fragment bound Ctp at a Panx:Ctp stoichiometry of 1:2 and with high affinity (KD = 0.1 µM±0.01 µM).
source: The wild-type Panx fragment bound Ctp at a Panx:Ctp stoichiometry of 1:2 and with high affinity (KD = 0.1 µM±0.01 µM) (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Ctp binding was completely abolished upon mutation of both TQT motifs in Panx.
source: In line with the co-immunoprecipitation analysis, Ctp binding was completely abolished upon mutation of both TQT motifs (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Each TQT site in Panx exhibited Ctp binding alone at a Panx:Ctp ratio of 1:1.
source: ITC for the same fragment containing mutations in either of the TQT motifs individually showed that each site exhibited Ctp binding alone at a Panx:Ctp ratio of 1:1 (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The first TQT site is bound with higher affinity than the second (KD = 0.7 µM±0.10 µM and KD = 0.2 µM±0.06 µM upon mutation of TQT#1 and TQT#2, respectively).
source: Both sites bind Ctp strongly, although the first site is bound with higher affinity than the second (KD = 0.7 µM±0.10 µM and KD = 0.2 µM±0.06 µM upon mutation of TQT#1 and TQT#2, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by ITC measurements.

claim: Panx2xTQT failed to rescue gypsy repression in cells depleted of endogenous Panx.
source: Panx2xTQT failed to rescue gypsy repression in cells depleted of endogenous Panx (Figure 4H), despite showing comparable expression levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G) and localising to the nucleus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), implying that Ctp is required for Panx to direct transposon silencing.
evidence: This is supported by rescue assay data shown in Figure 4H and expression/localization data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: Mutating TQT#1 had a stronger impact on the ability of Panx to rescue transposon silencing than mutation of TQT#2.
source: As predicted from higher affinity binding of Ctp to TQT#1 (Figure 4G), mutating this site had a stronger impact on the ability of Panx to rescue transposon silencing than mutation of TQT#2 (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by rescue assay data shown in Figure 4H and ITC data in Figure 4G.

claim: Panx2xTQT failed to induce silencing of the RNA tethering reporter in OSCs.
source: Consistent with an inability to repress transposons, Panx2xTQT also failed to induce silencing of the RNA tethering reporter in OSCs (Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I,J), suggesting that interaction with Ctp is required for silencing upon enforced recruitment to target RNA.
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I, J.

claim: Only Ctp was significantly depleted in the Panx2xTQT immunoprecipitation compared to wild-type Panx.
source: Lastly, comparing IP-MS for Panx with Panx2xTQT in OSCs showed that the effect of the mutation is highly specific. We did not find broad changes in the protein interactome of these constructs, with only Ctp significantly depleted in the Panx2xTQT immunoprecipitation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by IP-MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Panx, Nxf2, Ctp, and Egg, but not Piwi, were able to induce repression when recruited to the reporter locus in S2 cells.
source: Using the DNA tethering reporter assay, we found that Panx, Nxf2, Ctp, and Egg, but not Piwi, were able to induce repression when recruited to the reporter locus in S2 cells (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Tethering of both LacI-Panx and LacI-Egg resulted in substantial accumulation of H3K9me3 across the reporter sequence and a concurrent reduction in H3K4me2 coverage in S2 cells.
source: Compared to the LacI-Renilla control, tethering of both LacI-Panx and LacI-Egg resulted in substantial accumulation of H3K9me3 across the reporter sequence and a concurrent reduction in H3K4me2 coverage (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The ability of Ctp to induce reporter silencing in S2 cells was considerably weaker than that of Panx, with ~40% signal remaining upon transfection of LacI-Ctp compared to ~10% for LacI-Panx.
source: We noticed that the ability of Ctp to induce reporter silencing in S2 cells was considerably weaker than that of Panx, with ~40% signal remaining upon transfection of LacI-Ctp compared to ~10% for LacI-Panx (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overexpression of Panx but not the Panx2xTQT mutant with LacI-Ctp enhanced the level of reporter repression by fourfold.
source: In support of this, overexpression of Panx but not the Panx2xTQT mutant with LacI-Ctp enhanced the level of reporter repression by fourfold, resulting in comparable silencing to that caused by LacI-Panx itself (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Panx that is unable to interact with Ctp induced silencing to the same extent as wild-type Panx when recruited directly to a DNA locus.
source: To test whether Panx depends on the downstream recruitment of Ctp to induce epigenetic silencing, we tethered LacI-Panx2xTQT to DNA in S2 cells. Panx that is unable to interact with Ctp induced silencing to the same extent as wild-type Panx when recruited directly to a DNA locus (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F), indicating that Panx does not absolutely require Ctp to elicit transcriptional repression in this setting.
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: Panx self-associates in OSCs.
source: We observed via co-immunoprecipitation that Panx self-associates in OSCs (Figure 6A) and we therefore asked whether Ctp mediates this interaction.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Knockdown of ctp substantially reduced the co-immunoprecipitation of differentially tagged Panx proteins.
source: In control cells, HA-Panx but not HA-GFP was recovered when 3xFLAG-Panx was immunoaffinity purified, however knockdown of ctp substantially reduced the co-immunoprecipitation of the differentially tagged Panx proteins (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Differentially tagged Panx2xTQT proteins failed to associate in OSCs.
source: Moreover, differentially tagged Panx2xTQT proteins failed to associate in OSCs (Figure 6A), whereas mutation of the first motif alone impaired, but was not sufficient to abolish the interaction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nxf2 self-associated in OSCs in a manner dependent on its interaction with Panx.
source: Nxf2 also self-associated in OSCs in a manner dependent on its interaction with Panx, because it was disrupted by deletion of the UBA domain which mediates the Panx interaction (Figure 6C; Batki et al., 2019; Fabry et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6C and cited literature (Batki et al., 2019; Fabry et al., 2019).

claim: Artificial dimerisation of Panx2xTQT via fusion to a leucine zipper restored the ability of Panx to silence when tethered to RNA.
source: We reasoned that if the primary function of Ctp within PICTS is to promote complex dimerisation, and as such if the Panx2xTQT mutant failed to induce silencing when tethered to RNA due to a failure in self-association, then we could rescue this phenotype by enforcing dimerisation of Panx2xTQT via an alternative domain. To this end, we fused Panx2xTQT with a C-terminal leucine zipper from the S. cerevisiae transcription factor GCN4 (Goldman et al., 2019; Sladewski et al., 2018) which restored dimerisation of Panx2xTQT in OSCs (Figure 6F). Strikingly, tethering of this construct to RNA once again resulted in reporter repression (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C), indicating that the main function of Ctp within PICTS is to promote dimerisation of the complex.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 6F and reporter assay data in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C, and cited literature (Goldman et al., 2019; Sladewski et al., 2018).

claim: Artificial dimerisation of Panoramix bypasses the necessity for its interaction with Ctp.
source: Artificial dimerisation of Panoramix bypasses the necessity for its interaction with Ctp, demonstrating that conscription of a protein from a ubiquitous cellular machinery has fulfilled a fundamental requirement for a transposon silencing complex.
evidence: This is supported by the leucine zipper rescue experiment shown in Figure 6F, G.

claim: Ctp is an essential component of the PICTS complex.
source: Here, we report that the highly conserved dynein light chain LC8/Cut-up (Ctp) is an essential component of the PICTS complex.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experiments including IP-MS, knockdown phenotypes, and functional assays.

claim: Loss of Ctp results in transposon de-repression and a reduction in repressive chromatin marks specifically at transposon loci.
source: Loss of Ctp results in transposon de-repression and a reduction in repressive chromatin marks specifically at transposon loci.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Ctp can enforce transcriptional silencing when artificially recruited to RNA and DNA reporters.
source: In turn, Ctp can enforce transcriptional silencing when artificially recruited to RNA and DNA reporters.
evidence: This is supported by tethering assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Dimerisation of the PICTS complex is essential for heterochromatin formation and silencing.
source: Considered together, our data reveal that Ctp-mediated higher order PICTS complex assembly is essential for heterochromatin formation and silencing.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experiments including co-IP, rescue assays, and ChIP-seq data.

claim: The carboxy-terminal domain of Panx acts as a scaffold for PICTS complex assembly through its interaction interfaces with Nxf2 and Ctp.
source: Thus, our data point to a model in which the carboxy-terminal domain of Panx acts as a scaffold for PICTS complex assembly through its interaction interfaces with Nxf2 (bridging to Nxt1) and Ctp, while the largely disordered amino-terminal region is the driving force for transcriptional silencing through mechanisms that remain unresolved (Figure 6H; Batki et al., 2019; Fabry et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a model based on the data presented in the manuscript and cited literature (Batki et al., 2019; Fabry et al., 2019).

claim: Dimerisation-incompetent Panx fails to induce silencing when artificially recruited to RNA.
source: Dimerisation-incompetent Panx fails to induce silencing when artificially recruited to RNA (Figure 4I), while this mutant can trigger silencing to the same degree as wild-type Panx if tethered directly to DNA.
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 5E.

claim: When Panx is delivered to DNA via fusion to LacI, binding to the dyad symmetric lacO site effectively delivers the fusion protein as a tetramer.
source: It is, however, worth noting that when Panx is delivered to DNA via fusion to LacI, binding to the dyad symmetric lacO site effectively delivers the fusion protein as a tetramer (Friedman et al., 1995; Lewis et al., 1996).
evidence: This is based on cited literature (Friedman et al., 1995; Lewis et al., 1996) about LacI binding properties.

claim: Artificial recruitment of Panx to DNA in somatic cells that lack a functional piRNA pathway is able to elicit heterochromatinisation of the reporter locus.
source: Lastly, we found that artificial recruitment of Panx to DNA in somatic cells that lack a functional piRNA pathway is able to elicit heterochromatinisation of the reporter locus (Figure 5B,C), suggesting that the mechanisms and machineries operating downstream of Panx are not gonad-specific.
evidence: This is supported by reporter assay and ChIP-seq data in S2 cells shown in Figure 5B, C.

claim: Ctp depletion had a stronger impact on transposon (and gene) expression than depletion of Panx in both germline and somatic tissue.
source: Ctp depletion had a stronger impact on transposon (and gene) expression than depletion of Panx in both germline and somatic tissue.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing ctp and panx knockdowns shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The involvement of Ctp in transposon regulation may not be restricted to its role within PICTS.
source: We note that the involvement of Ctp in transposon regulation may not be restricted to its role within PICTS.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation that Ctp interacts with other chromatin regulators.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of Ctp from OSCs recovered a number of chromatin regulators including Wde and Egg.
source: Immunoprecipitation of Ctp from OSCs recovered a number of chromatin regulators including Wde and Egg.
evidence: This is based on IP-MS data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Wde contains a predicted Ctp recognition motif and therefore is likely a true partner of Ctp.
source: Wde contains a predicted Ctp recognition motif and therefore is likely a true partner of Ctp, highlighting the widespread presence of Ctp as a hub protein in a multitude of complexes.
evidence: This is based on LC8Pred analysis and inference from the IP-MS data.

claim: Binding of Ctp to the dynein intermediate chain promotes self-association of a nascent helix domain.
source: For example, binding of Ctp to the dynein intermediate chain promotes self-association of a nascent helix domain (Benison et al., 2006), and a similar mechanism has been proposed for Panx (Schnabl et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on cited literature (Benison et al., 2006; Schnabl et al., 2021).

claim: The transcription factor Asciz which is known to regulate Ctp expression was enriched in the Ctp IP-MS.
source: Lastly, the transcription factor Asciz which is known to regulate Ctp expression (Jurado et al., 2012; Zaytseva et al., 2014) was also enriched in the IP-MS and was previously linked to germline transposon silencing (Czech et al., 2013), a finding potentially explained by the implication of Ctp in this mechanism.
evidence: This is based on IP-MS data and cited literature (Jurado et al., 2012; Zaytseva et al., 2014; Czech et al., 2013).

claim: Ctp recognition sequences are well-conserved throughout putative insect Panx orthologs.
source: Ctp recognition sequences are well-conserved throughout putative insect Panx orthologs with some species such as the housefly, Musca domestica, and mosquito, Aedes aegypti, harbouring three predicted motifs compared to the two found in Drosophilids (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Complex dimerisation could be a conserved requirement for transcriptional repression in insects.
